outcome: As far as I can find, nothing since 26 January 2024 has moved the weak bound Q(N)=O(√N) or the strong form (the progression 24n+1 maximises the number of squares for every N ≥ 6), and the best exponent (Bombieri–Zannier, 2002) and the verified range (6 ≤ N ≤ 52, González-Jiménez–Xarles, 2013/2014) are unchanged. The only in-window items are a 2025 sumset-of-squares note that mentions the conjecture only as hopeless and says its author will withdraw it (Hegyvári, arXiv 2504.13230), and a November 2025 talk by S. Laishram advertising unspecified 'new results' on the Erdős–Rudin problem for a given progression length, for which I found no written version.
problem_asks: Rudin's conjecture on the number of squares in finite arithmetic progressions, unpacked from the statement and from the literature's standard form. (1) Q(N) is the maximum, over non-trivial arithmetic progressions qn+a (the literature takes q and a to be integers; the bullet does not say so), of the number of perfect squares among the N terms qn+a for 0 ≤ n < N. (2) Weak form, part (a): Q(N)=O(√N), i.e. there is a constant C with Q(N) ≤ C√N for all N. (3) Strong form, part (b): for every N ≥ 6 (González-Jiménez and Xarles write N ≥ 6; the Wikipedia text as my fetch summarised it reads N > 6, which differs only at N = 6), Q(N) = Q(N;24,1), i.e. the progression 24n+1 attains the maximum. Not asked by the bullet but found in the literature, and so treated as different questions: uniqueness of the maximising progression (the 'Super-Strong Rudin's Conjecture' of González-Jiménez–Xarles, for N = GP_k + 1 ≥ 8); analogues for ℓ-th powers with ℓ ≠ 2; the same question over number fields or quadratic extensions.

events.what_happened: Szemerédi proved Erdős's conjecture that the number of squares in an N-term arithmetic progression is o(N), as a consequence of his theorem on long arithmetic progressions: a set of positive density among the terms would contain four squares in arithmetic progression, contradicting Fermat's theorem that there are no four squares in arithmetic progression. Cilleruelo and Granville (2006) attribute the argument to Szemerédi. Sources give the year as 1969 (his four-element paper) or 1970; the squares application is not located in the 1969 paper by any source I could open.
events.delivers: Q(N)=o(N): a qualitative upper bound on the same quantity Q(N), with no rate. It is far weaker than the weak form O(√N) and says nothing about the strong form.
events.remains: The O(√N) bound (part a) and the claim that 24n+1 is extremal for N ≥ 6 (part b).

checked_by.what_they_did: Restate the argument with attribution to Szemerédi; I read this only through a search-result summary because the PDF body did not decode

events.direction: Upper bound o(N) on the quantity Rudin's conjecture bounds, so it points the same way as the conjecture but is much weaker.

events.what_happened: González-Jiménez and Xarles, 'On a conjecture of Rudin on squares in arithmetic progressions', first posted to arXiv on 22 January 2013 (arXiv 1301.5122; single version) and published as LMS Journal of Computation and Mathematics 17(1) (2014), 58–76, DOI 10.1112/S1461157013000259, online 1 April 2014. The abstract states that they prove Rudin's conjecture (Q(N)=O(√N), and in its stronger form Q(N)=Q(N;24,1) for N ≥ 6) for 6 ≤ N ≤ 52; that 24n+1 is the only progression up to equivalence attaining Q(N) at the N where Q(N) increases, for 7 ≤ N ≤ 52 (N = 8, 13, 16, 23, 27, 36, 41, 52); and they formulate a 'Super-Strong Rudin's Conjecture' for N = GP_k + 1 ≥ 8. The body of the paper was not readable with my tools, so the method is unverified.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 22 Jan 2013 only (per arXiv abstract page); journal version LMS JCM 17(1), 2014, online 1 Apr 2014.
events.delivers: Both claims of the problem for the finitely many N with 6 ≤ N ≤ 52: Q(N) = Q(N;24,1) (which gives the O(√N) form trivially for those N), and for 7 ≤ N ≤ 52 uniqueness of the maximising progression up to equivalence at the N where Q(N) increases. Restricted to the integers and to non-trivial progressions qn+a. The paper does not treat N > 52, and the O(√N) claim is not proved as an asymptotic statement.
events.remains: Every N > 52 (both the asymptotic O(√N) bound and the strong form for those N). Uniqueness for all N (the Super-Strong conjecture) remains a conjecture.

checked_by.who: LMS Journal of Computation and Mathematics and its (anonymous) referees
checked_by.qualification: A refereed research journal of record
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the paper (online 1 April 2014). No named post-publication verification, review or write-up found; the Cambridge page lists no reviews

events.directly_checkable: For each N in 6..52 the claim is a finite statement about progressions qn+a. Checking it needs the reduction that limits which (q,a) must be tested; that reduction is the paper's content, which I could not read, so I cannot say how a reader would check it by hand.
events.direction: Proves the two claims of the conjecture for 6 ≤ N ≤ 52, so it cuts the same way as the statement for those N. It gives no information for N > 52.
events.object: The progression 24n+1 (terms 1, 25, 49, 73, 97, 121, …; its square terms sit at indices that are generalized pentagonal numbers, since 24·k(3k−1)/2 + 1 = (6k−1)²). It is explicit. The paper states that it attains Q(N) for the stated N, and that no other progression, up to equivalence, does so at the increase points for 7 ≤ N ≤ 52. Those optimality claims are the paper's finite verifications; the method is not read.

events.what_happened: Cilleruelo and Granville, 'Lattice points on circles, squares in arithmetic progressions and sumsets of squares', arXiv math/0608109 (3 August 2006; one version, labelled a preliminary version). The abstract opens with Rudin's conjecture (at most c·N^{1/2} squares in an N-term progression) and says the authors formulate more than twenty conjectures in harmonic analysis, number theory, arithmetic geometry, discrete geometry and additive combinatorics that would each shed light on it. The body suggests the extremal progression is 49 + 24i for 1 ≤ i ≤ k once k ≥ 8, giving √(8k/3)+O(1) squares. The conjectures are not results. The PDF body did not decode, so this comes from the abstract and from search summaries of the body.
events.revisions: v1 3 Aug 2006 only (per arXiv abstract page). Later AMS volume 'Additive Combinatorics' (2007) cited in search summaries; not checked.
events.delivers: Nothing proved about Q(N). Records the conjectural extremal progression 49 + 24i (the same family as 24n+1 once 49 = 24·2+1) and more than twenty conjectures that would bear on Rudin's conjecture.
events.remains: All of the problem: the O(√N) bound (part a) and the claim that 24n+1 is extremal for N ≥ 6 (part b).
events.direction: Conjectures only. Its conjectured extremal progression 49 + 24i agrees with the strong form's 24n+1 family; it asserts nothing about whether Rudin's bound holds.

events.what_happened: Bourgain and Demeter, 'On the number of kth powers inside arithmetic progressions', arXiv 1811.11919 (v1 29 Nov 2018; v2 7 Dec 2018, which the comment says gives a simpler argument for all powers). The abstract states sharp upper bounds for the number of kth powers inside arbitrary arithmetic progressions whose step has O(1) divisors. This is an analogue for general powers and a restriction on the steps, not a count of squares in every progression.
events.revisions: v1 29 Nov 2018; v2 7 Dec 2018 (per arXiv abstract page).
events.delivers: Sharp bounds for kth powers in progressions whose step has O(1) divisors. For k = 2 this covers only squares in progressions with such steps, so it does not bound Q(N) over all steps. It is not about the 24n+1 maximum.
events.remains: The count of squares over all steps q (so part a in full), and the strong form (part b). The paper's exact constants were not read.
events.direction: Upper bounds for a restricted class of progressions and for general k. It does not bear on the direction of Rudin's conjecture for squares over all steps.

events.what_happened: Hajdu and Tengely, 'Powers in arithmetic progressions', Ramanujan Journal 55(3) (2021), 965–986, DOI 10.1007/s11139-020-00331-5 (online 2020). It characterises the progressions containing the most ℓ-th powers asymptotically (unique up to equivalence for each ℓ ≥ 2, with two for ℓ = 4, as one search summary of a companion paper reports), formulates Rudin-type analogues for general ℓ, and, per a seminar abstract by Hajdu (Austrian–Hungarian Diophantine seminar; Rényi listing dated 22 January 2021), proves them for ℓ = 3 up to N = 19 and ℓ = 4 up to N = 5. I did not open the paper, so these ranges come from the seminar abstract only.
events.delivers: Analogues of Rudin's conjecture for ℓ-th powers with ℓ ≥ 3 (ℓ = 3 up to N = 19, ℓ = 4 up to N = 5, per the talk abstract). The square case ℓ = 2 is Rudin's own conjecture, so this adds nothing to Q(N) for squares.
events.remains: For squares, all of the problem: parts (a) and (b) as stated.

events.object: The extremal progression for ℓ-th powers, which the seminar abstract describes as the 'best' progression, unique for any ℓ. Its formula was not read.

events.what_happened: Hegyvári, 'Note on the sumset of squares', arXiv 2504.13230 (v1 17 April 2025; v2 22 April 2025). The main result is a lower bound |Q+Q| ≥ C′|Q|(log|Q|)^{1/3+o(1)} for finite non-empty sets Q of squares. The abstract says this 'essentially is proved – with the same tools – by Mei-Chu Chang' (J. Funct. Anal. 207 (2004), 444–460) and that 'the author will withdraw this ArXiv file'. Remark 3 of Section 3 reads, in part: 'In 1960 Rudin conjectured, that in any N-term arithmetic progression the number of square numbers is ≪√N (see in [4]). The proof of this conjecture still seems hopeless today.' Its bibliography entry [4] is Rudin, 'Trigonometric series with gaps', 1960. The remark cites no other work on the conjecture in the parts I read.
events.revisions: v1 17 Apr 2025; v2 22 Apr 2025 (per arXiv; html v2 read). The abstract states intent to withdraw. No withdrawal notice seen on the abstract or html pages on 13 October 2026.
events.delivers: Nothing on Q(N). Its sumset bound concerns |Q+Q| for sets of squares, a different quantity, and the author says Chang already proved it. Rudin's conjecture appears only as motivation.
events.remains: All of the problem: parts (a) and (b).
events.doubts: The author concedes in the abstract that the main result is essentially Chang's (2004) and states an intent to withdraw the file. The remark's 'seems hopeless' is an opinion with no argument attached, and it is not a result on the conjecture.

withdrawn.what: The abstract says 'So the author will withdraw this ArXiv file.' No withdrawal was visible on the abstract or html pages read on 13 October 2026, so it may be a stated intent rather than a completed withdrawal.

events.direction: No direction on the conjecture. The remark asserts nothing either way; it calls the proof 'hopeless'.

summary: I searched for Rudin's conjecture under its name, with its variants, with words a result would use, and with AI terms, and I opened what the searches returned where the pages would load. Nothing I found since 26 January 2024 settles the problem, moves the best exponent for Q(N), or extends the verified range. The problem's status is therefore open, and the in-window material is thin. Two items are in window. Hegyvári's 'Note on the sumset of squares' (arXiv 2504.13230, April 2025) is about sums of squares. It mentions Rudin's conjecture in Remark 3 as motivation, calls its proof 'hopeless', and its abstract says the author will withdraw it. Here I had conflicting readings: my first fetch of the abstract page did not mention Rudin, but the html version does, and I read Remark 3 directly. The second is a November 2025 talk by Laishram (BIMSA 6 Nov; Rényi 21 Nov) that advertises 'some results on a related conjecture of Erdős and Rudin on the number of squares in an arithmetic progression of a given length'. The abstract does not state the results, and I found no preprint, slides or arXiv listing for it (the author listing returned 404). This is the lead most likely to matter, and the record can't say what it contains. The landmark results all predate the window: Szemerédi's o(N) (1969 or 1970), Bombieri–Granville–Pintz (1992, exponent 2/3), Bombieri–Zannier (2002, exponent 3/5), and González-Jiménez–Xarles (arXiv January 2013, published 2014) proving both parts for 6 ≤ N ≤ 52. For GJX I read the abstract and the journal page; the body did not decode. Several 2026 papers look close but are out of scope: squares over quadratic extensions of number fields (arXiv 2602.03251 and 2602.01380, the first not opened); Dietmann–Elsholtz on two-dimensional progressions avoiding squares (2605.11104, opened); Korsky on hitting sets for k-term progressions (2606.01780, opened); and Novaković on inhomogeneous powers in progressions (2606.14340, opened). I also checked Ramaré (2501.05056) and Granville (1708.06951), which are not about counting squares in progressions. For AI I found nothing: no source names a system in connection with this problem, and the AI-contributions wiki (teorth/erdosproblems) has no entry for it, nor does the erdosproblems.com 'arithmetic progressions' tag list the squares problem (its only squares entry is #192, about abelian squares). The neighbouring AI-related items I found are about other problems: an OpenAI proof of the Erdős–Turán conjecture on arithmetic progressions, posted in September 2026 and reported in the Computational Complexity blog on 11 October 2026 (a different problem, not recorded as an event); the May 2026 OpenAI disproof of the planar unit-distance conjecture; and several Aristotle/GPT-5.x Erdős solutions. Close calls for the judging pass: (i) whether a finite verification for 6 ≤ N ≤ 52 settles any part of the problem, or only adds instances of a universal claim; (ii) whether the Laishram results, whatever they are, would move Q(N) for N beyond 52; (iii) whether Szemerédi's o(N) counts as bounding the same quantity (it does, weakly); (iv) whether Bombieri–Zannier's argument targets progressions containing four squares, as one summary says, which I could not verify.
competing_reading: The strongest case for the other reading is that the Laishram talk is a live, in-window advance on the Erdős–Rudin problem. A 2025 talk advertising 'new results' on the squares-count conjecture could be a bound or a verification extending past N = 52, and that would be the only in-window event. Its title and abstract are specific, and it is listed at two institutes. Against this: the abstract says what the results concern, not what they establish, and I found no written version, which means I cannot say the talk moved anything. Reading the GJX verification as a settlement would count six to fifty-two cases of a universal claim as progress. The stronger reading treats those cases as a finite census that moves nothing, which is the rule used for Collatz and the 1-3-2-3 conjecture. Reading Hegyvári's remark as evidence the problem is 'open and not cited' is also available: the remark cites only Rudin 1960 and ignores GJX's verified range, which weakens the note's own account of the state of the problem.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The Laishram talk slides, abstract, or any preprint from 2025–2026, with the theorems stated; the arXiv author listing (arxiv.org/a/laishram_s_1) was unreachable, so an arXiv search by author name is needed. (2) The full text of González-Jiménez–Xarles (arXiv 1301.5122), to see the reduction that limits which (q,a) need testing, and so whether the 6 ≤ N ≤ 52 result is a complete finite verification of both parts for those N. (3) The Hegyvári arXiv listing over time, to see whether the withdrawal happens and whether Remark 3 is changed. (4) The erdosproblems.com entry for the σ(k) = o(k) problem, to see whether it links Rudin's question and what status it shows. (5) The formal-conjectures repository (google-deepmind/formal-conjectures), to see whether a Lean statement of Rudin's conjecture exists and whether it is marked solved or sorry-containing; a GitHub code search needed a login I do not have. (6) A zbMATH or MathSciNet record of the 2014 journal review, to confirm whether the paper was reviewed beyond journal acceptance.

events.credibility_reason: Author concedes the main result is essentially Chang (2004) and states intent to withdraw; it contains nothing on Q(N) anyway.

judgement.why: All substantive events predate the snapshot. Szemerédi's o(N), Bombieri–Granville–Pintz's N^{2/3+o(1)} and Bombieri–Zannier's N^{3/5+o(1)} are upper bounds on Q(N) that leave the O(√N) claim open: bound, digested through journal publication (Szemerédi's argument via the published restatement by Cilleruelo–Granville). González-Jiménez–Xarles verify both forms for 6 ≤ N ≤ 52 only. That is a finite range of a statement about all N, so it is instances, not a case; this was the close call. The ℓ-th-power and restricted-step papers are variants. Cilleruelo–Granville poses conjectures only, so its scope is none. The two in-window items settle nothing. Hegyvári mentions the conjecture only as motivation. Laishram's talk abstract states no result, so it supports no scope above none. No AI is involved anywhere.
judgement.doubts: The Laishram talk (November 2025) advertises results on the Erdős–Rudin problem for a given length, but no written version was found. If those results extend the verified range or move the exponent, this verdict would understate in-window movement. The Hajdu–Papp verification rests on journal publication known only from a search summary.
